hints: Look first at the lower curve labelled 'with enzyme' and trace it from its starting level on the left up to its own peak.
Remember activation energy is always measured from the energy of the starting reactants up to the top of the curve for that reaction.
walkthrough:
**Recall what activation energy means**

Think of it as the energy hill the reactants must climb to get started. It is measured from the starting energy level of the reactants up to the very top (peak) of the curve.

Rule to use:
$$activation\ energy = energy\ of\ peak - energy\ of\ reactants$$

**Apply this to the with-enzyme curve**

The 'with enzyme' curve is the lower one, because enzymes lower the hill. Its starting point is the lowest dashed line on the left. Its peak is the middle dashed line. The vertical distance between those two lines is labelled B.

**Confirm by eliminating the rest**

The higher peak belongs to the reaction without enzyme, so any distance up to that top peak is not the enzyme-catalysed value. That leaves B as the only distance from reactants to the enzyme-lowered peak.

options.A: A only shows the difference between the two peaks, so it shows how much the enzyme lowers activation energy, not the activation energy itself.
options.B: B goes from the reactant starting energy up to the peak of the 'with enzyme' curve, which is exactly the activation energy of the enzyme-catalysed reaction.
options.C: C goes from the reactant starting energy up to the higher peak, so it is the activation energy of the reaction without enzyme.
options.D: D is a much larger distance from the product level up to the peak level, so it does not measure the hill climbed from the reactants.
